body: A man of thirty-eight is at the kitchen table with a laptop, watching a video his sister has sent him, because she has sent it twice now. It is well made. About ninety seconds in, a man on screen is telling a story about his father, and just before it lands the music comes up underneath — strings, low, on the second beat of the sentence. He knows that move. He has done that move himself, for eleven years, writing appeal emails for a charity that does genuinely good work. He watches the rest with his arms folded, guesses where the ask is coming, and is right within four seconds. He shuts the laptop and goes to put the bins out.

Whatever was true in that video did not reach him, and a good deal of it may well have been true. He was not disagreeing with any of it. He had recognised the shape, and once a person can see the shape, the content stops arriving.

Anybody who has spent time near modern Christian media can feel the machinery. The story that turns. The pause before the appeal. The music arriving under the sentence that matters. Techniques borrowed almost entirely from direct marketing, and they work, in the narrow sense that they produce a response.

The word close is worth taking literally, because it is a technical term and means what it says. In sales, a close is not the moment a person decides. It is the moment their deciding is brought to an end. That is the craft of it: the assumed close that proceeds as though agreement had already happened, the urgency close that makes waiting expensive, the takeaway that removes an option to make it desirable. Every one of them works by shortening the interval in which somebody is still free to think. That is not a slur on the people who use them, most of whom are sincere. But the mechanism does not care what is loaded onto it, and what it does, in every case, is close.

The policy holds across every frequency under this beat, on a dial running from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70. No countdown. No urgency that was manufactured rather than real. No story engineered so that the turn lands on a request.

That is an expensive commitment, and expensive in the one currency this sort of work is usually measured in. Every technique named above exists because it lifts response, and lifting response is how budgets get defended in any organisation that has to raise money. Refusing them means the numbers will always look worse than they need to, and there is no clever way round it. The argument for doing it anyway is short. If a thing is true, it does not need a technique. If it needs a technique, that is worth noticing about the thing.

There is now a whole generation that reads media the way a locksmith reads a door. They are not cynical about the message; they are fluent in the format, and fluency cannot be switched off. Every surface they meet wants something — the app that waits until the third session before it asks, the advert that holds on a face two beats longer than it needs to. The cost of that is not irritation. It is that sincerity has become unreadable. When everything is shaped like an appeal, the things that are not shaped like one are the only ones with any chance of being heard as true.

In practice the policy is a list of things that do not happen. Music does not swell under a request. The schedule is published before it airs, so nothing is arranged around what a listener did last week. Nothing is described as ending soon unless it is ending soon. The rotation runs the same whether ten people are listening or ten thousand, because a station that changes its behaviour the moment it senses an opportunity is a station that has been reading you.
None of which is an argument against ever asking anybody for anything. That would be a different article and a much sillier one.

Be fair to the case for urgency, because it is a serious one. A preacher who never asks anything of anybody has arguably not preached. Scripture is full of appeals and some are extremely direct — now is the accepted time, and choose this day. Urgency is not always manufactured; sometimes it is simple honesty. But the technique spends something that does not belong to the person using it. Every manufactured deadline teaches a listener that deadlines here are decoration, and the lesson generalises. Somebody who has learned to hear the pause before the appeal cannot unhear it, and when a real appeal arrives, from somebody else, years later, it is inaudible in exactly the same way.
Technique borrows against the credibility of everybody who comes after you.

A girl of nineteen is working a Saturday market stall in the rain, selling her aunt’s cheeses, and the man on the next stall sells plants and is about sixty. It is slow. They talk on and off for four hours about the weather, the parking, somebody’s van. At some point he says, with no run-up, that he had a bad couple of years after his wife died and would not have got through them without his church, and that he still does not entirely understand what happened to him then. Then he sells somebody a fuchsia. He asks her nothing about it and does not mention it again, and at four they pack the stalls away. She thinks about that sentence, on and off, for most of October.

Nothing was being attempted there, which is the only reason it landed. He was not building towards anything, so there was nothing for her to defend herself against, and the sentence went in the way an ordinary true sentence does.

The cost of working this way is real. Measured on response, this loses to the machinery every single time, and anybody who says otherwise is selling a technique of their own. People who would have moved under pressure will not move. Some will drift off the frequency, and nothing will happen, and there will be no way of knowing which ones they were. A method that refuses to engineer outcomes has to live with the outcomes it gets, and some months those are thin.

But response is the wrong measure and has been for a long time. A decision produced by technique has to be maintained by technique, which is why the same names come forward at the same events year after year and everybody involved knows it. What is built under pressure comes apart when the pressure is removed, because the pressure was the structure. What a person arrives at slowly, in their own time, with nobody watching, is load-bearing, and needs nobody to keep pushing it.

So the policy is not modesty, and not a marketing position dressed as humility. It is a bet about what holds. If what is broadcast here is true, it can survive being stated plainly, at ordinary volume, to somebody free to switch it off, and it does not require the listener to be hurried. If it cannot survive that, no amount of strings underneath the sentence makes it truer, and all the technique will have achieved is a response nobody can keep.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them. The schedule for all of it is published in advance, which is the plainest test of the policy there is: nothing can be timed to catch you if you can see it coming.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 376.20 — Melody’s Sparkle. Its format is pre-evangelistic pop, an ugly phrase for a straightforward idea: songs about gratitude, family and ordinary wonder, written to be playable to somebody who is not in church and may never be. Clean, warm, and not preachy. It follows from the argument above more directly than anything else here, because it is a format defined by what it declines to do. It does not make the ask. It does not build to a turn. It is a station you could leave on with the window open. If this article is right, that is not a weaker form of the work; it is the work, at the speed people actually move at.

Practically: there is nothing to install, no app and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever is nearest and press play — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. There is an account if you want one. It keeps your favourites with you across the Jubilee sites, and it is how the band learns which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next station gets built; it will matter more later than it does today. That is the whole of the practical section and it is deliberately dull.

This is the paragraph in which an article of this kind asks you for something, and the shape of the page rather expects it. There is nothing here. The frequency is HM 376.20, it is playing now, and it will be playing in March whether you tune in or not. If you do and it is not for you, turn it off; nothing will follow you about it. That is not modesty either. It is the same policy as the rest of the station, applied to the one paragraph where it would be most tempting to make an exception.
